newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris Moslem immigrants fear harassment after bomb.
newsitem.headline: Paris Moslem immigrants fear harassment after bomb.

text.p: North African immigrants in Paris on Thursday predicted months of police checks and suspicious stares in a new security alert imposed in France after a commuter train bombing by suspected Algerian Moslem extremists.
"It's racial discrimination," said Taillebe Becaoui, a 20-year-old unemployed man of Moroccan origin in Paris' heavily immigrant Goutte d'Or district.
"If you look like an Arab, police will check your identity papers. If you're blond, never. And the government says it hasn't ruled anything out in its hunt for the bombers," he said.

Moslems in the depressed area unanimously condemned the bombing on a Paris rush-hour train on Tuesday in which two people died and 91 were injured, but they worried about a repeat of months of checks and what they saw as harassment after a wave of bombings in 1995.

They all grumbled about suspicious looks from fellow Parisians on the Metro or buses, especially if they were carrying a bulky package. France has sent 1,800 troops on to the streets to reinforce police and gendarmes.

No one has claimed responsibility for Tuesday's blast but Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre said there were worrying similarities to last year's attacks by Algerian Moslem militants that killed eight people and injured more than 160 others.

"The checks are annoying but maybe it has to be like that," said Abid Houarri, a 21-year-old Algerian on his way to pray at a mosque where a Moslem cleric was shot dead last year in a killing that heralded the bombing campaign.
"People who want to go to pray wearing traditional Moslem dress are scared to go into the streets," he said outside the Rue Myrha mosque, which is protected by crash barriers.

The Armed Islamic Group (GIA) claimed responsibility both for last year's bombs and for killing Sheikh Abdel-Baki Sahraoui, 85, an imam who was co-founder of Algeria's less radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).
An Algerian working in an Islamic butcher's shop along the street said: "Sure, the checks are annoying. Extra security helps everyone, but it's wrong that it's always directed at people like us."
"Whenever there's suspicions of terrorism it's the Africans and the Arabs -- the black faces -- who get stopped," he added, declining to give his name. "It's wrong to demonise people."

Separately, the Paris-based International Federation of Human Rights Leagues (FIDH) said it had appealed to the Foreign Ministry after Paris denied a visa to the head of the Algerian rights league, Ghechir Boudgema, to visit Paris this weekend.
"He's come several times without problems in the past. We are very surprised and wonder if this is a mistake," a FIDH spokesman said. Boudgema was to attend a meeting on human rights in Arab nations.
Some Paris Moslems said life was hardest for immigrants whose documents were not in order and who were forced deeper into hiding.

One man said a positive spinoff was that people of North African origin made sure they bought Metro rail tickets during the checks, rather than indulging in an unofficial national sport of hurdling ticket barriers.
